introduction.text: **Before you start.** This is the largest course of the program: eight culinary traditions, each studied through the same lens and cooked in four lessons (history and pantry, two signature techniques, and a meal). It is taught in two sections, each a unit of progress:

items.text: **`CUI-3.SEC1` Europe and the Mediterranean** (`CUI-3.M1`–`M5`): the lens, then French regional, Italian, Iberian, and Levantine and North African cooking;
**`CUI-3.SEC2` Asia and Mexico** (`CUI-3.M6`–`M9`): the Indian subcontinent, Chinese, Japanese and Mexican cooking.

introduction.text: A section is complete when the assessments of its modules are passed; `MS-S3` and `CUI-4` need the whole course.
*The lens.* Every tradition is studied with the same five questions (`CUI-3.M1.L1`): the pantry; the core techniques; the flavour profile; the meal structure and drinks; history and geography.

*Respect and adaptation.* Each tradition is regional and alive. The course teaches representative dishes and the logic behind them, not a single "authentic" version. Adaptations to a Dutch kitchen are allowed and named:

items.text: **produce:** Dutch seasonal vegetables stand in where the original is out of season or flown in (pointed cabbage or chard for Chinese greens; Dutch greenhouse peppers and tomatoes in summer; pumpkin and roots in winter). Every substitution is noted in the exercise, with its effect;
**pantry goods** (spices, rice, noodles, soy sauce, miso, *masa harina*, chillies, olive oil) come from specialist shops, which `CUI-3.M1` maps;
**meat and fish** are Dutch or North Sea, by the rules of the earlier courses.
minced fillings and poultry to 75 °C; fish to 63 °C for 15 seconds; no raw-fish dishes here (`GRD-3.M3` has the rules);
cooked rice cooled fast and kept cold;
raw-yolk sauces with pasteurised egg; soft-set egg dishes and cured meats not served to risk groups;
allergens (sesame, peanuts, tree nuts, soy, fish, crustaceans, gluten) named for guests.

introduction.text: Plan twelve to fifteen weeks, roughly one tradition every one and a half weeks, with the section boundary as a natural pause. Most dishes are household meals; each tradition ends with a meal, several with guests.

**Have ready:** the pantry map (`CUI-3.M1.X1`); the lens template; the flavour plan and component table (`FLV-3`); the scales and the probe; a wide frying pan or *paella* pan; a pasta machine or a long rolling pin; a wok; a heavy flat pan or *tawa*; a rice pan with a lid; a mortar and pestle; the household and guest cards; the journal.

note.text: **Knowledge check:** the 8 items of `CUI-3.M1` in the course file. Pass mark 80 %.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** eight traditions are too many to memorise as recipes. Five questions, asked the same way each time, turn them into patterns you can recognise, compare and cook from.
**You need:** a cookbook or a set of recipes from a tradition you don't know; the lens template; the spice notes of `FLV-3.M2`; the journal.
**Explanation:**
*The five questions:*

items.text: **the pantry:** the fats, starches, aromatics, acids and condiments that recur;
**the core techniques:** the methods that define the cooking;
**the flavour profile:** the balance of tastes and aromas that makes a dish "taste of" the tradition;
**the meal structure and drinks:** how a meal is put together, served and eaten, and what is drunk with it;
**history and geography:** why the tradition is as it is: climate, trade, religion, migration.

blocks.text: *Start at home.* Apply the lens first to the cooking you know best, Dutch home cooking: butter; potatoes and *stamppot*; the *hachee* braise; mustard and vinegar; the evening meal of meat, potatoes and vegetables; coffee and a *koekje*. The lens is clear before it meets the unfamiliar.
*The pantry as a fingerprint.* A tradition can often be recognised from its fat, its starch, its aromatic base and its acid:

items.text: butter, wheat, shallot and wine;
olive oil, wheat or rice, garlic and tomato;
ghee, rice and wheat, onion, ginger and spices, tamarind or yoghurt;
neutral oil, rice, ginger, garlic and spring onion, soy and rice vinegar;
lard or oil, corn, chilli and lime.

blocks.text: *Meal structure and drinks.* Courses in sequence (France, Italy); many dishes at once (China, India, the Levant); a set tray (Japan). Water, wine, beer, tea or fresh drinks with the meal: at this level, knowing what is usually drunk.
*History and geography as explanation.* Trade routes (spices; chillies from the Americas), religion (pork, beef, fasting), climate (preserving, fats). A date matters only if it explains a dish.
*Reading for the lens.* Read a cookbook or recipe from the tradition for what it assumes the cook already knows.
**Practice:** theory only (1.5 h): fill in the lens for Dutch home cooking, then for one tradition of the course from a cookbook; list three things the cookbook assumes you know.
**Look for:** for any tradition in the course, you can name its fat, starch, aromatic base and acid.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: A country taken for a tradition
A tradition judged by its takeaway
Restaurant versions abroad as the model
Read home cookbooks from the tradition
History as a list of dates
Keep only the history that explains a dish

blocks.text: **Safety:** none in this lesson; each tradition's safety points are in its own lessons.
**Record:** the lens for Dutch home cooking and for one tradition.

**Why it matters:** a recipe from another tradition leaves out what every home cook there knows, and uses measures and names you don't. Reading it well, and knowing where to shop, decides whether the dish works.

**You need:** two recipes from different traditions (for example an American and an Indian one); the scale; a pen; a phone for photos; a specialist shop near you (Asian, Turkish, Moroccan, Surinamese or Mexican).
**Explanation:**

*Implicit technique.* Recipes leave out what every home cook in that tradition knows: "fry the *masala* until the oil separates", "cook the rice", "make a *sofrito*", "add *dashi*". Recognise the gap and fill it from the lens and the course.
*Converting conventions:*

items.text: **cups and spoons to grams,** by ingredient: a US cup holds about 240 ml, so a cup of water weighs about 240 g, a cup of flour roughly half that, a cup of sugar about 200 g;
**Fahrenheit to Celsius:** subtract 32, multiply by 5, divide by 9; gas marks and fan ovens by your oven's table;
**names:** US cilantro is coriander leaf; "scallions" are spring onions;
**pans and equipment:** a wok, a *paella* pan, a *tawa*, and what you have instead.

blocks.text: *Finding errors.* Check a recipe whose ratio, time or quantity doesn't make sense against what you know: three tablespoons of salt for 500 g of rice; 10 minutes for a beef shin.

*Sourcing.* Which ingredients are in a Dutch supermarket, which at an Asian, Turkish, Moroccan, Surinamese or Mexican shop, which online. Note sensible substitutes and their effect, and what to buy whole and in small amounts (`FLV-3.M2`): a large bag of a spice used once goes stale on the shelf.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Two recipes (45 min).** Two recipes from different traditions read, converted to the program's conventions, and annotated with the implicit steps.
**A shop visit (60 min).** One specialist shop near you visited; the shelves photographed; the key pantry items for two traditions noted with prices.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: every cup turned into grams;
every implicit step written in;
a sourcing list with shops and substitutes.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Cups of flour converted as 250 g
Write implicit steps into the recipe
A large bag bought for one dish

blocks.text: **Safety:** imported pantry goods carry allergen labels in other languages: check them, or buy a brand with a Dutch or English label, for every allergic guest (`SAF-1.M4`).
**Record:** the two annotated recipes and the shop notes with prices.

exercises.title: A pantry map and a sourcing list
exercises.description: A pantry map of the eight traditions; a sourcing list for the shops near you.

blocks.text: **Task:** map the pantries of the eight traditions, and prepare to source them near home. Fill in a pantry map of the eight traditions (fat, starch, aromatic base, acid, key condiments and spices) and a sourcing list for the shops near you, with prices, substitutes and Good or Best choices. Analyse three unfamiliar pantry ingredients from the map in writing (for example sumac, *katsuobushi* and *masa harina*) and cook each in a small dish. Adapt two recipes from other countries' conventions to the program's; one has three planted errors to find and correct, with a reason.
**You need:** the course's tradition notes; the pantry-map template; shop visits or websites; small amounts of the three ingredients; the two recipes (one with planted errors, from the course set).
**Recipe:** the map and the list.

items.text: **Fill in** the pantry map: one row per tradition; fat, starch, aromatic base, acid, condiments, spices.
**Visit or browse** the shops; write the sourcing list with shop, price, a substitute and its effect, and Good or Best.
**Analyse** the three unfamiliar ingredients: what each is, how it tastes, how it is used.
**Cook** each in a small dish (for example sumac on roasted onions, *katsuobushi* in a quick broth, *masa harina* as a small flatbread); photograph.
**Adapt** the two recipes: weights, Celsius, names, equipment; find and correct the planted errors with a reason.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`JD-CHSE` level 3:** three unfamiliar ingredients analysed in writing and cooked by a chosen approach; each result acceptable.
**`CK-RCPT` level 4:** at least two of three planted errors found and corrected with a reason (and the items at 80 %); a recipe adapted from another country's conventions.
**`IN-SEL` level 4, further evidence:** sourcing with quality, price and purpose noted; the row was met in `VEG-3.M1.X1`.

blocks.text: AI review reads the map, the list and the adapted recipes: *competent* is eight complete rows, a list with prices and substitutes, and at least two errors found with reasons; *not yet* is a map with gaps, or errors passed.
**Time:** 3 h, plus the shop visits.

items.question: Which is not one of the five questions of the lens?
Ghee, rice and wheat, onion, ginger and spices, with tamarind or yoghurt as the acid, point to which tradition?
Which tradition usually serves many dishes at once to share?
Why are chillies so common in Indian, Chinese and Thai cooking today?

options.text: they arrived from the Americas through trade after the 16th century

items.question: A recipe says "fry the *masala* until the oil separates". What does it assume?

options.text: that the cook knows the onion-spice base must cook down until the oil seeps out at the edges

items.question: How is "1 cup flour" converted?

options.text: by the ingredient's weight per cup (flour about 120–130 g)

items.question: A recipe for 500 g of rice says "3 tbsp salt, cook 5 minutes, 2 l water for absorption". Which errors do you find?
items.answer: All three are off: far too much salt (about a teaspoon is usual), far too short for most rice (often 12–18 minutes), and too much water for an absorption method (about 1–1.5 times the rice by volume, by variety).
items.why: Planted errors in ratio, time and quantity.

items.question: Where would you most likely find *masa harina* and dried *ancho* chillies?

options.text: a Mexican or Latin-American shop, or online

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** the classical French cooking of `SAU-2` grew from regional home and inn cooking. Seeing France as regions, each with its own fat and produce, explains its dishes far better than a list of famous recipes.
**You need:** mussels (in season, by `FSH-2`); cider from Dutch or French apples; dry white wine; butter; olive oil; shallots; garlic; tomatoes; parsley; two pans with lids; the lens template.
**Explanation:**
*France as regions.* Each region is shaped by its fat, its produce and its neighbours:

items.text: **Normandy:** butter, cream, apples and cider, Calvados; *poulet vallée d'Auge*, mussels in cider;
**Burgundy:** red wine, beef, mustard, snails; *bœuf bourguignon*, *œufs en meurette*;
**Provence:** olive oil, garlic, tomatoes, herbs, fish; *ratatouille*, *aïoli*, *bouillabaisse*;
**the South-West:** duck and goose fat, confit, beans; *cassoulet*, *pommes sarladaises*;
**Alsace:** lard, cabbage and sauerkraut, pork, Riesling; *choucroute garnie*, *tarte flambée*.

blocks.text: *Terroir.* The idea that place shapes taste: cheese, wine, butter and poultry sold with a named origin.
*The lens applied:*

items.text: **pantry:** butter, oil or duck fat; shallots; wine; herbs;
**techniques:** braising, *sauté*, emulsions, pastry;
**flavour profile:** rich, rounded, herb-scented;
**meal structure:** *entrée*, *plat*, cheese, dessert;
**drinks:** a regional wine or cider, and water.

blocks.text: *Dutch kitchen notes.* Normandy and Alsace match Dutch produce closely: apples, cabbage, pork and dairy. Provence is best cooked in summer, with Dutch greenhouse tomatoes, courgettes and peppers.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A regional tasting (60 min).** Mussels two ways side by side: Normandy-style in cider and butter with shallots, and Provence-style in white wine with olive oil, garlic and tomato; tasted and described with the lens.

blocks.text: **Look for:** you can place a French dish in its region from its fat and produce.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Restaurant food taken as the cuisine
A Normandy dish that tastes southern
Match the fat to the region
Two dishes that taste the same
Change the fat, the liquid and the herbs

blocks.text: **Safety:** mussels by the rules of `FSH-2`: closed or closing when tapped before cooking, cooked until open; shellfish is an allergen to name for guests (`SAF-1.M4`).
**Record:** the lens notes for both mussel dishes.

**Why it matters:** cooking one regional dish properly, with its accompaniments and its place in the meal, teaches more about a region than reading about ten. Adapting it honestly to what you can buy is the judgment.
**You need:** a French regional cookbook or reliable sources; the ingredients of the chosen dish, Dutch and in season; the lens template; the household cards.
**Explanation:**

*Choosing a dish.* One regional dish with its accompaniments, researched with the lens: its region, its fat, its produce, its place in the meal. Choose for the season, not for fame: a *choucroute garnie* in winter, a *ratatouille* in late summer, chicken in cider and cream in autumn when the apples come in.
*Adapting to local ingredients.* Three kinds:

items.text: **what can be bought in the Netherlands in season:** often most of it;
**what is substituted:** cider from Dutch apples; a Dutch farmhouse cheese for a regional one; pointed cabbage for a regional cabbage. Name each substitution and its effect;
**what can't be:** if the core of the dish isn't available, it isn't that dish any more, so its name changes ("in the style of").

blocks.text: *The write-up against the lens.* One page that places the dish: its region, fat and produce, its techniques, its flavour profile, its place in the meal, the drink, and the history that explains it; then the adaptations and their effects.
*Cooking it.* Use the techniques of the earlier courses: the braise of `SLW-3`, the sauce work of `SAU-2`, the pastry of `PST-3`. Note which you used and where.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Research and plan (60 min).** The dish chosen and researched; the adaptations written.
**Cook (2 h).** The dish and its accompaniments cooked; household cards.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a dish a French home cook would recognise, with every adaptation named.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Choose from what the season offers
A dish that isn't what it claims
Name each; rename the dish if its core changed
A page of history, no cooking logic
Fill every question of the lens

blocks.text: **Safety:** the dish follows the §9 figures of its ingredients (poultry 75 °C; a braise cooled by the standard if made ahead); an *aïoli* is made with pasteurised egg.
**Record:** the lens page, the adaptations and their effects, and the cards.

lessons.title: Butter, cream, olive oil and duck fat

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** the cooking fat is the quickest key to a French region. Cooking one dish from each side of the butter-oil line shows how the fat shapes the heat, the sauce and the balance of a dish.

**You need:** for the butter dish: chicken thighs, leeks or potatoes, butter, cream, cider or white wine, shallots; for the oil or duck-fat dish: summer vegetables and olive oil, or waxy potatoes, duck fat and garlic; the probe.
**Explanation:**
*How the cooking fat shapes a cuisine:*

items.text: **butter and cream** (the north and west): rich, rounded sauces; browned butter; gentle heat, because butter burns;
**olive oil** (the south): fruity and peppery, good for high heat, and raw as a finish;
**duck and goose fat** (the South-West): savoury, for crisp potatoes and confit;
**lard** (Alsace and the centre): pork dishes and pastry.

blocks.text: *One dish from each side:*

items.text: **a butter-and-cream dish:** chicken in cider and cream, leeks in cream, or a *gratin dauphinois*;
**an oil or duck-fat dish:** a *ratatouille* in summer, or *pommes sarladaises*: sliced potatoes fried slowly in duck fat, finished with garlic and parsley.

blocks.text: *The fat in the flavour profile.* The fat carries the aromatics: shallot and thyme in butter, garlic and herbs in oil. It also needs balance: acid, wine or mustard to cut the richness. Taste each dish for it.
*Browned, not burnt.* Butter foams, then turns golden and smells of hazelnuts (*beurre noisette*); a moment later it burns. Take it off the heat at golden and pour it into a cool bowl.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The butter dish (75 min).** A dish from Normandy or Burgundy.
**The oil or duck-fat dish (75 min).** A dish from Provence or the South-West.

blocks.text: **Look for:** each dish tastes of its fat and its region.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Off the heat at golden; into a cool bowl
Olive oil heated past its smoke point
Moderate the heat; add the oil to a warm pan
No acid to balance the fat

blocks.text: **Safety:** chicken to 75 °C (§9); hot fat handled with dry tools; potatoes fried in fat added to the pan carefully, away from you.
**Record:** both dishes, the fat and its balance, and a photo of each.

**Why it matters:** a French home meal is a sequence, and its pleasure is in the proportions: a light start, a satisfying main, cheese or dessert, and a cook who sits at the table. Planning makes that possible.

**You need:** the menu from one region; the components prepared ahead where possible (a braise, a terrine from `GRD-3`, a tart from `PST-3`); bread; a regional wine or cider, and water; the guest cards.
**Explanation:**
*The French home meal:*

items.text: **an *entrée*:** a salad, a soup or a terrine;
**a *plat*** with its garnish;
**cheese or dessert,** or both;
bread on the table throughout; water and a regional wine, or cider.

blocks.text: *Order, portions and drink:*

items.text: **a light *entrée* before a rich *plat***: a leek vinaigrette before a *bœuf bourguignon*, not a cream soup;
**modest portions** per course, so each is welcome;
**the cheese before the dessert,** with the bread;
**the drink from the same region:** cider with Normandy, a Burgundy red with a Burgundy braise, or a non-alcoholic choice on the same lines.

blocks.text: *Planning.* Most of the meal is prepared ahead: a braise improves overnight, a terrine is made days before, a tart's components the day before. On the day, only the garnish and the assembly remain, so you sit at the table.
*An example, Normandy in autumn:*

items.text: **entrée:** a salad of chicory and apple with a cider vinaigrette;
**plat:** chicken in cider and cream with buttered leeks;
**cheese:** a Dutch soft cheese in place of Camembert, named;
**dessert:** an apple *tarte fine* (`PST-3.M2.L3`).

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: **The meal (3 h).** A three-course meal from one region for the household or guests.

blocks.text: **Look for:** portions that leave room for the next course; the courses flowing.
**If it goes wrong:**
**Safety:** components made ahead are cooled by the standard and reheated until steaming hot throughout; cheese and cold dishes are out of the fridge for at most 2 hours (§9).
**Record:** the menu, the timeline, the portions and the cards.

**Task:** cook a three-course dinner from one French region from frameworks, recognisably of its place. Write a flavour plan per course, with the regional fat and produce and every adaptation to Dutch produce named, and the write-up against the lens. Collect household or guest cards, including whether they recognise the style. Analyse in writing one regional ingredient new to you, and cook it.
**You need:** the region's dishes, with Dutch seasonal produce; a regional or comparable drink; the lens template; the flavour plans; the guest cards.
**Framework:** the regional dinner.

rows: One region, its fat and produce
Pantry, techniques, flavour profile, meal structure and drinks, history
Regional, or a named Dutch substitute

blocks.text: *Procedure:*

items.text: Choose the region; write the lens page, the menu and the flavour plans.
Prepare ahead; cook; serve in order.
Collect cards on balance and recognition; review.

blocks.text: **Show:**

items.text: **`CK-CUIS` level 3, the French part:** the tradition quiz at 80 % and two dishes from frameworks that the style description and the tasters recognise (this dinner and `CUI-3.M2.X2`).
**`FL-ARCH` level 3, further evidence:** dishes with written flavour plans; the tasters find depth and balance.
**`JD-CHSE` level 3, further evidence:** a new regional ingredient analysed and cooked; the row was met in `CUI-3.M1.X1`.

blocks.text: AI review reads the lens page, the plans and the cards: *competent* is a menu that fits its region and season, named adaptations, and tasters who recognise the style; *not yet* is a mixed-region menu, or unnamed substitutions.
**Time:** 4 h.

Your planned French dinner is a creamy soup, a *bœuf bourguignon* and a chocolate mousse. What would you change?

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** Italian home cooking is built on few, good ingredients, matched to their region and season. Its pasta logic, the right shape with the right sauce, finished together, changes how you cook pasta every week.

**You need:** dried pasta (spaghetti or a short shape); good olive oil; garlic; tomatoes (summer) or a tin of good tomatoes; butter; Parmigiano Reggiano or Grana Padano; salt; a large pot; a wide pan; tongs.
**Explanation:**
*North against south:*

items.text: **the north:** butter, rice (*risotto*), polenta, fresh egg pasta, cured meats;
**the south:** olive oil, dried durum-wheat pasta, tomatoes, vegetables and fish.

blocks.text: *Cucina povera.* Cooking from few, humble ingredients made good: bread soups, beans, greens, pasta with breadcrumbs, using everything. It is close to the whole-vegetable cooking of `VEG-3`.
*Pasta and sauce logic:*

items.text: **the shape matches the sauce:** long and flat with butter and cream or a *ragù*; tubes and ridges with chunky sauces; small shapes in soups;
**finished in the sauce:** drained a minute early, tossed in the pan with the sauce and a little of the starchy cooking water until glossy and clinging;
**sauced, not drowned.**

blocks.text: *Meal structure.* *Antipasto*; *primo* (pasta, rice or soup); *secondo* (meat or fish) with a *contorno* (vegetables); *dolce*. At home, often only *primo* and *secondo*. Wine and water at the table, an espresso after.
*Few ingredients, high quality.* The best olive oil, cheese and tomatoes you can find. Dutch summer tomatoes and winter greens fit: *cavolo nero* grows well in the Netherlands.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Two pastas (60 min).** A southern dried-pasta dish (tomato, garlic and olive oil) and a northern butter-and-cheese pasta; compared with the lens.

blocks.text: **Look for:** the pasta finished in the sauce, glossy and clinging.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Finish the pasta in the sauce with cooking water
Never rinse; the starch binds the sauce

blocks.text: **Safety:** a large pot of boiling water is drained at the sink, the colander in place first and the pot tipped away from you. Parmigiano and pasta contain milk and gluten (`SAF-1.M4`).
**Record:** both pastas, the lens notes, and a photo of the sauced pasta.
**Why it matters:** fresh egg pasta is flour and eggs, and the difference between a silky ribbon and a thick, gummy one is in the kneading and the rolling. Rolled evenly, it cooks evenly.

**You need:** Italian "00" flour (or a mix with semolina); eggs; semolina for dusting; a pasta machine or a long rolling pin; a ruler; a sharp knife; a clean tea towel; a large pot; butter and Parmigiano for the sauce; the scale.
**Explanation:**

*The dough.* Flour and eggs by weight: the classic is roughly one egg per 100 g of flour, adjusted by feel. Make a well in the flour, break the eggs into it, beat them with a fork, and draw in the flour little by little. Knead 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic, like a soft earlobe. Wrap it and rest it for 30 minutes, so the gluten relaxes.
*Rolling.*

items.text: **by machine:** pass the dough through the widest setting, fold it in three, and pass it again a few times until smooth; then through each setting in turn;
**by hand:** with a long pin, rolling from the centre and turning the sheet;
**to an even thickness:** thin enough to see the shadow of a hand through it for tagliatelle, thinner for filled pasta; check it against a ruler.

blocks.text: *Cutting.* Tagliatelle (about 6–8 mm), *pappardelle* (wider), *lasagne* sheets. Dust them with semolina and toss them loosely into nests, so they don't stick.
*Cooking.* In plenty of well-salted boiling water for one to three minutes; drained a moment early and finished in the sauce.
*Storage.* Dried in nests for a day, or frozen. Cooked fresh pasta is treated as leftovers: in the fridge within 2 hours, eaten within 2 days (§9).
**Practice:**

items.text: **Make and roll (75 min).** A batch of dough made and rested, rolled to two thicknesses, photographed against a ruler.
**Cut and cook (60 min).** Tagliatelle cut and cooked, finished in a simple butter sauce; the thickness and bite judged.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: a smooth, elastic dough;
even sheets that show the hand's shadow;
cooked in minutes, with bite.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Knead in flour a spoon at a time
Fold and pass on the widest setting; roll every sheet to the same setting

blocks.text: **Safety:** raw dough contains raw egg: wash hands and the board after handling. Egg and gluten are allergens (`SAF-1.M4`).
**Record:** photos of the sheets against the ruler and the cooked pasta; notes on bite.

**Why it matters:** filled pasta and *gnocchi* are where Italian home cooking turns leftovers and potatoes into something special. Both depend on technique more than ingredients: a seal without air, a light hand with flour.

**You need:** fresh pasta dough (`CUI-3.M3.L2`); a filling of ricotta and greens, or roasted pumpkin and Parmigiano; floury potatoes (*kruimig*); flour; butter; sage; a potato ricer; a pastry wheel or knife; a slotted spoon; a small brush and water.
**Explanation:**

*Filled pasta.* A thin sheet; a filling that is dry and well seasoned (ricotta and greens, pumpkin, mushrooms, a braise); sealed without air pockets, because air expands and bursts them. Brush the edges with a little water or egg wash and press out the air around each mound. Shapes:

items.text: **ravioli:** squares or rounds, two sheets or one folded;
***tortellini*:** small squares folded into triangles, wrapped around a finger and joined;
***agnolotti*:** a strip folded over a line of filling and pinched.

blocks.text: *Fillings.* Raw meat fillings are avoided at this level. Cooked fillings (a braise from `SLW-3`) are cooled before use and kept as leftovers. Drain ricotta and squeeze greens well: a wet filling soaks the dough.

*Light gnocchi.* Floury potatoes, baked or steamed (not boiled wet), riced while hot, with as little flour as will hold them, mixed briefly. Waxy potatoes and extra flour make them dense and gluey (`STA-1`). Cook one test dumpling first: if it falls apart, add a little flour; if it holds, cook the batch. Ricotta *gnocchi* use drained ricotta, egg and a little flour.
*Cooking.* In gently boiling water; lift them out a moment after they float. Finish them in butter and sage, or a light sauce.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Ravioli and *tortellini* (75 min).** A ricotta-and-greens or pumpkin filling; two shapes; cooked and served.
***Gnocchi* (60 min).** Potato *gnocchi* from floury potatoes; a test dumpling cooked before the batch; finished in brown butter.

blocks.text: **Look for:**

items.text: filled shapes that hold, with no bursts;
light *gnocchi* that keep their shape.

blocks.text: **If it goes wrong:**

rows: Press the air out around each mound
Drain ricotta; squeeze greens; cool cooked fillings
Kneaded like bread, or too much flour
Mix briefly; test one; add flour only if needed

blocks.text: **Safety:** cooked fillings cooled by the standard before use; ricotta *gnocchi* contain egg and milk (`SAF-1.M4`).
**Record:** photos of the shapes and the *gnocchi*, the test dumpling, and the amount of flour used.
**Why it matters:** an Italian meal is a balance between its courses: a *primo* that opens the appetite, a *secondo* that is still welcome. Getting the proportions right is the skill.
**You need:** the menu: a *primo*, a *secondo* with a *contorno*, a *dolce*; seasonal Dutch produce; the scale for the pasta portions; the timeline; the guest cards.
**Explanation:**
*The Sunday meal:*

items.text: **a *primo*:** pasta or *risotto*;
**a *secondo*** of meat or fish: a roast, a braise, grilled fish;
**a *contorno*:** seasonal vegetables;
**fruit or a simple *dolce*.**

blocks.text: *Proportions between the courses:*

items.text: **a modest *primo*:** about 80 g of dried pasta or 100 g of fresh per person, so the *secondo* is still welcome;
**the *contorno*** served on its own plate or beside, not as a garnish on the meat.

blocks.text: *When one simple sauce is enough.* A *primo* with one sauce of few ingredients, done well (butter and sage; tomato and basil; *cacio e pepe*-style cheese and pepper), rather than a complex one competing with the *secondo*. Keep the complexity in one course.

*Timing.* The *secondo* goes in the oven, or rests, while the *primo* is eaten; the pasta is cooked at the last moment. A braise can be made the day before. Write the timeline backwards from when the *secondo* is served.
*An example, in late autumn:*

items.text: **primo:** fresh tagliatelle with butter and sage;
**secondo:** pork shoulder braised in milk, or a chicken roasted with rosemary;
**contorno:** *cavolo nero* with garlic and olive oil;
**dolce:** pears poached in red wine.

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: **The meal (3 h).** A *primo*, a *secondo* with *contorno*, and a *dolce* for the household or guests.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a light *primo*, a welcome *secondo*, the courses timed.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: A huge plate of pasta first
80 g dried or 100 g fresh per person
Plan the vegetable as a course
One rich course; the other simple

blocks.text: **Safety:** the *secondo* cooked to its §9 figure (poultry 75 °C; pork as intact meat 63 °C for 15 seconds, or a braise until tender); leftovers in the fridge within 2 hours (§9).
**Record:** the menu, the portions as weighed, the timeline, and the cards.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** Spanish and Portuguese cooking is built from a short pantry used with confidence: olive oil, paprika, a slow *sofrito*, cured pork and salt cod. Knowing what each does lets you cook the dishes and recognise them.
**You need:** sweet (*dulce*) and smoked *pimentón*, two olive oils, a cured sausage (*chorizo* or *chouriço*), a Spanish or Portuguese cheese, bread; the lens template; tasting forms.
**Explanation:**
*The pantry:*

items.text: **olive oil** for everything, from frying to finishing;
***pimentón***, Spanish paprika, smoked or sweet, *dulce* or *picante*; with saffron, garlic and parsley;
***sofrito***: onion, garlic, peppers and tomato cooked slowly in olive oil until jammy, the base of rice dishes, stews and sauces;
**cured pork:** *jamón*, *chorizo*, *lomo*; in Portugal *chouriço* and *presunto*;
**salt cod** (*bacalao*, *bacalhau*): salted and dried, soaked before cooking, central to Portuguese cooking;
**staples:** short, round, absorbent rice such as *bomba*; chickpeas and beans; almonds; sherry vinegar.

blocks.text: *Tapas culture.* Small dishes, hot and cold, shared standing or at the table, with a drink. It is a way of eating rather than a set of recipes.
*The lens applied:*

items.text: **techniques:** a slow *sofrito*, rice in a wide pan, frying in olive oil, the *plancha*;
**flavour profile:** smoky paprika, garlic, olive oil, saffron;
**meal structure:** a late lunch as the main meal, tapas in the evening;
**drinks:** wine, sherry, *vinho verde*, water.

blocks.text: *Paprika burns.* Ground paprika turns bitter in seconds in hot oil. Add it off the heat, or with the liquid, and taste smoked against sweet before choosing: smoked paprika everywhere flattens every dish into one.

*Cured meats.* Dry-cured hams and sausages are raw animal foods: they are in the risk-group row of §9. Name them for pregnant guests, young children, older people and anyone with lowered immunity, and offer a cooked alternative.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A pantry tasting (45 min).** Sweet against smoked *pimentón* (a pinch of each warmed briefly in oil off the heat, tasted on bread), two olive oils, a cured sausage and a cheese. Describe each with the lens.

blocks.text: **Look for:** you can name the *sofrito*, tell the two paprikas apart, and say what cured pork brings to a dish.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Sweet paprika by default; smoked where the dish asks for it
Off the heat, or with the liquid
Use the five questions for each item

blocks.text: **Safety:** cured meats named for risk groups (§9); the cheese and sausage back in the fridge within 2 hours.
**Record:** the tasting form, the lens notes, and the shop where each item came from.

**Why it matters:** a *paella*-style rice is cooked without stirring, in a thin layer, and finished with a crust on the bottom. Each of those is the opposite of a *risotto*, so the rice and the method have to be chosen together.

**You need:** a wide, shallow pan (a *paella* pan or the widest frying pan you have); *bomba* or *calasparra* rice and a risotto rice for the comparison; a stock; saffron, *pimentón*; seasonal vegetables; the probe; the scale.
**Explanation:**
*The method:*

items.text: Make a *sofrito* in the pan.
Brown the main ingredients.
Add a well-flavoured stock (fish, chicken or vegetable) with saffron, and bring it to the boil.
Scatter the rice in an even, thin layer.
**Do not stir** from here on. Cook until the liquid is absorbed and the grains are tender but separate.

blocks.text: *The* socarrat. In the last minutes, raise the heat and listen. When the bottom crackles, a thin, caramelised crust forms: crisp and toasty, not burnt. Lift a corner with a spoon to check, and take the pan off the heat when it smells toasty, before it smells burnt.

*The rice.* Short, round, absorbent rice (*bomba*, *calasparra*) takes up a lot of liquid and stays firm. Risotto rice releases more starch and goes creamy, which is wrong here. Choose the variety and write down why (`IN-STA`).

*A home stove.* A pan wider than the burner heats unevenly: the middle cooks and the edge stays wet. Move and turn the pan, set it over two burners, or finish the rice in the oven. Note which adaptation you used, and how the grains at the edge compared with the middle.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A vegetable rice (75 min).** A wide-pan rice with seasonal vegetables (green beans in summer; pumpkin and chickpeas in autumn), the *socarrat* made.
**A comparison (60 min).** The same dish made with *bomba* and with risotto rice. Compare the texture, and photograph a spoonful of each.

blocks.text: **Look for:** an even, thin layer of rice; separate grains; a crackling, golden *socarrat*.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Raw grains on top, mush below
A thin layer; a wider pan or two pans
Listen for the crackle; check a corner; stop at toasty
Turn the pan, use two burners, or finish in the oven

blocks.text: **Safety:** chicken browned and cooked through to 75 °C; fish and other seafood to 63 °C (§9). Leftover rice cooled fast and kept cold (`SCI-2.M6`): into the fridge within 2 hours, eaten within 2 days.
**Record:** the rice varieties, the liquid and its ratio, the stove adaptation, and the two photos.
**Why it matters:** the slow *sofrito* is the flavour base under much of Iberian cooking; the *tortilla* tests egg cookery; and salt cod is the Portuguese staple that needs a day of planning.

**You need:** onions, peppers, garlic, tomatoes and olive oil for the *sofrito*; potatoes, onion and eggs for the *tortilla*; a non-stick pan and a plate wider than it; prawns, mushrooms or potatoes for the tapas; salt cod, soaked a day ahead; the probe.
**Explanation:**

*A slow* sofrito. Cook onions, peppers and garlic gently in plenty of olive oil for 30–45 minutes, until soft and sweet. Add grated tomato and cook it down until jammy and the oil separates. Make a batch and freeze it in portions.
*The* tortilla española:

items.text: Confit sliced potatoes and onion slowly in olive oil, until soft but not coloured.
Drain them, mix with beaten eggs, and rest for a few minutes.
Cook in the pan over medium heat, shaking it, until set at the edges.
Slide it onto a plate, invert it back into the pan, and cook the second side.

blocks.text: It can be set at the edges and soft in the centre, or set through. **A soft-centred *tortilla* is not served to risk groups (§9);** for them, cook it through.
*Two hot tapas,* for example:

items.text: ***gambas al ajillo*,** prawns in garlic oil, cooked to 63 °C;
***patatas bravas*** or ***champiñones al ajillo***.

blocks.text: *Salt cod:*

items.text: soak it in cold water **in the fridge** for one to two days, changing the water several times, until it tastes pleasantly seasoned;
poach it gently: it flakes when done. Use it in *brandade*-style dishes, fritters or a *bacalhau* bake;
handle it as raw fish until it is cooked.

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: ***Sofrito* and *tortilla* (90 min).** A batch of *sofrito*; a *tortilla* turned with a plate.
**Tapas and salt cod (75 min, after a day's soaking).** Two hot tapas; salt cod fritters or a salt cod bake.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a jammy, sweet *sofrito*; a *tortilla* that holds its shape when cut; salt cod pleasantly seasoned, not salty.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Not set at the edges, or a small plate
Wait for the edges; a plate wider than the pan
Too short a soak, the water not changed
Longer, with more changes; taste a flake

blocks.text: **Safety:** salt cod soaked in the fridge, never on the counter; prawns to 63 °C; the soft *tortilla* not served to risk groups (§9); crustaceans and egg named for guests.
**Record:** the *sofrito* time, the *tortilla* (soft or set, and for whom), the soak time and water changes.
**Why it matters:** a tapas evening is several dishes with different holding times. Hot and cold dishes have to arrive at their best, and the cold ones have a limit on the table.
**You need:** the menu; the timeline; the fridge space for the cold dishes; the probe; the guest cards.
**Explanation:**
*Two formats:*

items.text: **A tapas evening:** four to six small dishes, hot and cold, plus bread, olives and a drink. The cold dishes are ready ahead; the hot ones are finished in a sequence.
**A Portuguese family meal:**
a soup: *caldo verde*, kale and potato, a good match for Dutch kale in winter;
a centre dish: a salt cod bake, a pork and clam dish, or grilled sardines in season;
rice or potatoes, and a salad.

blocks.text: *Timing hot and cold dishes so that they arrive together:*

items.text: cold dishes plated and kept in the fridge until they go out, then on the table for at most 2 hours (§9);
hot dishes ordered by how long they hold: a stew holds, prawns don't. The stew is made first and kept hot; the prawns go in the pan at the last moment;
the last dishes are cooked while the first are eaten. A tapas evening is meant to arrive in waves.

blocks.text: *The timeline.* Write it backwards from when the guests arrive. Mark which dishes are done the day before (the *sofrito*, the soaked salt cod, a cold dish that improves overnight), which are done that afternoon, and which are cooked to order. Note the time each cold dish leaves the fridge.
**Practice:**

items.text: **The meal (3 h).** A tapas evening or a Portuguese family meal for the household or guests, on a written timeline.

blocks.text: **Look for:** hot dishes arriving hot, cold dishes cold, and no long gaps.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Everything arrives at once and goes cold
Order by holding time; send dishes in waves
Note the time out; back in the fridge, or away, at 2 hours
More done ahead; one hot dish per wave

blocks.text: **Safety:** cold dishes out for at most 2 hours (§9); prawns and chicken probed; cured meats and soft egg named for risk groups; the allergens on the table named.
**Record:** the timeline against the actual times, the time out for each cold dish, and the cards.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** the cooking of the Levant and the Maghreb balances sour, herbal, rich and warm-spiced flavours on one table. A handful of pantry items carries each of those, and most keep for months.
**You need:** tahini, sumac, *za'atar*, preserved lemon, pomegranate molasses; flatbread and thick yoghurt; Aleppo or *pul biber* chilli flakes if you can get them; the lens template; tasting forms.
**Explanation:**
*The pantry:*

items.text: **tahini,** sesame paste, for sauces and dips. Sesame is one of the allergens you name for guests;
**sumac** (sour, red, lemony), ***za'atar*** (`FLV-3.M2`), **Aleppo or *pul biber*** chilli flakes;
**preserved lemon:** salt-cured; the peel is used, chopped, in tagines and salads;
***ras el hanout*** (a North African spice blend) and ***harissa*** (a chilli paste);
**pomegranate molasses** (sweet-sour); **orange blossom and rose water** for sweets;
**staples:** olive oil, chickpeas, lentils, bulgur, couscous, flatbreads, yoghurt and *labneh*.

blocks.text: *The flavour profile.* Four elements, balanced across the table rather than in one dish:

items.text: **sour:** lemon, sumac, pomegranate;
**herbal:** parsley, mint, coriander and dill, used in quantity, as an ingredient;
**rich:** tahini, olive oil, lamb;
**warm-spiced:** cumin, cinnamon, allspice.

blocks.text: *Two regions, one lens:*

items.text: **the Levant** (Lebanon, Syria, Palestine, Israel, Jordan): mezze and grills;
**the Maghreb** (Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia): tagines, couscous and *harissa*.

blocks.text: *Meal structure and drinks.* Many dishes on the table, with bread as the utensil. Mint tea, water and *ayran*, a salted yoghurt drink.

*Two habits to drop.* Preserved lemon is mostly about the peel: a little chopped peel goes a long way, and the flesh in quantity makes a dish salty and bitter. And the herbs are a main ingredient: *tabbouleh* is a herb salad with a little bulgur, not a bulgur salad with herbs.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A pantry tasting (60 min).** Sumac, *za'atar*, preserved lemon peel, pomegranate molasses and tahini, tasted on bread and yoghurt. Describe each with the lens, and sort it into sour, herbal, rich or warm.

blocks.text: **Look for:** you can name the sour, herbal, rich and warm elements, and say which item carries which.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Whisk in lemon juice and water a little at a time; it loosens

blocks.text: **Safety:** sesame named on the tasting form, and for every guest later in the module; the yoghurt back in the fridge within 2 hours (§9).
**Record:** the tasting form, the sorting into the four elements, and where each item was bought.
**Why it matters:** a mezze spread is a composition: several small dishes that together give colour, texture, temperature and taste. Five beige dips are not a spread.
**You need:** dried chickpeas, tahini, lemons, garlic, ice water; an aubergine or beetroot; parsley, mint, bulgur; the centre's ingredients; bread; a blender; the component table (`FLV-3`).
**Explanation:**
*The parts of a spread:*

items.text: **dips:**
hummus: chickpeas cooked very soft, blended with tahini, lemon, garlic and ice water until silky;
*baba ghanoush* or *mutabal*: charred aubergine;
*muhammara*: roasted peppers with walnuts, or a nut-free version with bread and seeds, and pomegranate molasses;
**salads:** *tabbouleh* (mostly parsley), *fattoush* (with toasted bread and sumac), a shredded cabbage or carrot salad in winter;
**a centre:** grilled meat or vegetable skewers, *falafel*, or a braise;
**bread** and pickles.

blocks.text: *Silky hummus.* The chickpeas must be soft enough to crush between two fingers with no resistance. Undercooked chickpeas give grainy hummus whatever the blender. Blend the tahini, lemon and ice water first, then the warm chickpeas, and blend for longer than seems needed.
*Balancing a spread.* Fill in the component table for the whole table:

items.text: **colour:** green herbs, red peppers, purple beetroot, not all beige;
**texture:** smooth dips, crisp bread, a crunchy salad;
**temperature:** something hot beside the cold dips;
**taste:** sour, herbal and rich all present.

blocks.text: *Seasonal adaptations.* Dutch greenhouse aubergines and peppers in summer; in winter, cabbage, carrots, beetroot and pumpkin (a beetroot dip, roasted pumpkin with tahini).
**Practice:**

items.text: **Dips (90 min).** Hummus from dried chickpeas, and a charred aubergine or beetroot dip; silky and balanced.

**Why it matters:** a tagine is a braise with little liquid, where the pot's shape gives a concentrated sauce. Couscous steamed in two stages is a different food from the quick pour-over kind, and the difference is worth tasting once.

**You need:** lamb shoulder or chicken legs (or vegetables); onions, ginger, saffron, cinnamon, cumin, *ras el hanout*; dried apricots or prunes, or Dutch apples or pears; preserved lemon and olives; a tagine with a heat diffuser, or a heavy casserole with a tight lid; couscous; a steamer or a sieve over the pot; the probe.
**Explanation:**

*The tagine* is both the pot and the dish. The conical lid returns condensed steam to the food, so little liquid is needed. Meat or vegetables cook slowly with onion, spices, a little liquid, fruit, preserved lemon and olives.

*How the pot shapes the braise.* Little liquid plus the cone's condensation gives a concentrated sauce that coats. On a home stove, a heavy casserole (`HEA-2`) with a tight lid works the same way. A clay tagine needs a heat diffuser and gentle heat.
*Layering spices* (`FLV-3.M2`):

items.text: **at the start:** ginger, cumin, cinnamon and saffron, bloomed with the onions;
**at the end:** *ras el hanout* and fresh herbs, for the top notes.

items.text: Moisten the grains and rub them with oil.
Steam over the stew, or in a steamer, for about 15 minutes.
Turn them out, sprinkle with salted water, and break up the lumps with your fingers.
Steam again until fluffy.

blocks.text: The quick method (boiling water poured over, covered, forked) is the shortcut. Taste the two side by side.
*Doneness.* Lamb is done when it is tender to a fork. Chicken is cooked to 75 °C.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** "Indian food" is a subcontinent of cuisines, and "curry powder" flattens all of them. A few core terms (*tadka*, *masala*, *dal*) and a map of the regions are enough to start cooking with intent.
**You need:** split red lentils, turmeric, salt; ghee or oil; cumin seeds, garlic, mustard seeds, curry leaves, dried chilli; a small pan for the *tadka*; the lens template; tasting forms.
**Explanation:**
*A subcontinent of cuisines:*

items.text: **north:** wheat breads (*roti*, *naan*, *paratha*), dairy (ghee, *paneer*, yoghurt, cream), rich gravies, tandoor cooking;
**south:** rice, lentils, coconut, curry leaves, mustard seed, tamarind; *dosa*, *idli*, *sambar*, *rasam*;
**east:** mustard oil, fish, *panch phoron* (a five-seed blend), sweets from fresh cheese;
**west:** Gujarati sweet-sour vegetarian cooking, Goan vinegar-and-chilli dishes, Maharashtrian spice blends.

blocks.text: Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka share and extend these traditions.
*Core terms:*

items.text: ***tadka*** (*tarka*): whole spices, with garlic, curry leaves or chilli, fried in hot ghee or oil and poured over a dish at the end;
***masala***: a spice mixture, or the cooked base of onion, ginger, garlic, tomato and spices;
***dal***: split pulses, and the dish made from them;
**breads and rice** as the base of the meal.

blocks.text: *Meal structure and drinks.* Several dishes with rice or bread, eaten together. Water and *lassi* with the meal; tea (*chai*) outside meals. Many households are vegetarian, for religious or family reasons; ask your guests.

*The Dutch connection.* Surinamese-Hindustani cooking (*roti* with *masala* chicken, potatoes and long beans) is a living Indian-descended tradition in the Netherlands, and its shops are a good source for the pantry: whole spices, *atta* flour, lentils and basmati.
*The* tadka *goes on at the end.* Its aroma is strongest in the minutes after it hits the dish. Stirred in long before serving, it fades into the background (`CUI-3.M6.L3` explains why).
**Practice:**

items.text: **A spice and *dal* tasting (60 min).** A simple *dal* (red lentils simmered with turmeric until soft, salted), divided in three: one with no *tadka*, one with a cumin-and-garlic *tadka*, one with a mustard-seed-and-curry-leaf *tadka*. Taste them side by side, and place each regionally.

blocks.text: **Look for:** you can say what a *tadka* adds, and which region uses which.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Whole spices, chosen for the region
Pour it over at the table
Added with the seeds to very hot fat
Seeds first; garlic when they crackle; seconds only
Mustard seeds stay hard and bitter

blocks.text: **Safety:** hot fat poured away from you, in a small pan with a handle; curry leaves and mustard seeds spit, so stand back.
**Record:** the three *dals* tasted, the lens notes, and the regional placing.
**Why it matters:** a curry is built in stages, and each stage has a sign that tells you it is done. Rushing one stage gives a raw-tasting, flat sauce that no amount of spice at the end will fix.

**You need:** whole spices (cumin, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, bay); ground turmeric, coriander and chilli; onions, ginger, garlic, tomatoes; the main ingredient (chicken thighs, *paneer*, chickpeas or seasonal vegetables); yoghurt or coconut milk; *garam masala*, fresh coriander; the probe.
**Explanation:**
*Building a* masala:

items.text: **Whole spices** (cumin, cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, bay) bloomed in oil or ghee.
**Onions** cooked slowly to deep golden. This is the longest stage, and pale onions give a raw-tasting sauce.
**Ginger-garlic paste** fried until the raw smell goes.
**Ground spices** (turmeric, coriander, chilli) fried briefly, with a splash of water so they don't burn.
**Tomatoes** cooked down until the oil separates at the edges: the sign that the *masala* is done.

blocks.text: *The sauce.* The main ingredient simmers in the *masala* with water, stock, yoghurt or coconut milk. Finish with *garam masala* and fresh coriander, or a *tadka*.
*Balancing heat and acid:*

items.text: chilli added in steps, tasted between (`FLV-3.M2.L4`);
acid from tomato, yoghurt, tamarind, lemon or vinegar;
a pinch of sugar or jaggery to round;
salt last, once the sauce has reduced.

blocks.text: *Yoghurt.* Yoghurt boiled hard splits into curds and whey. Take the pan off the boil, stir it in a spoonful at a time, and keep the sauce below a boil from then on.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A *masala* (60 min).** The base built step by step; the "oil separates" stage photographed.
**The curry (90 min).** A chicken, *paneer* or vegetable curry from the *masala*, balanced, and finished with a *tadka* or *garam masala*.

blocks.text: **Look for:** deep golden onions; the oil separating at the edges; balanced heat and acid.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Onions not cooked to deep golden
Give the onions the time; low heat, stirring
Ground spices burnt in hot oil
A splash of water with them; seconds, not minutes
Off the boil, spoon by spoon; no boiling after
In steps; balance with yoghurt, acid or sugar

blocks.text: **Safety:** chicken to 75 °C (§9); dairy (ghee, yoghurt, *paneer*) named for guests; leftovers in the fridge within 2 hours.

**Why it matters:** *dal*, rice and bread are the base of the meal. Each has a clear standard: creamy *dal*, long and separate grains, soft breads that puff.

**You need:** split red lentils, yellow split peas (*toor* or *chana*) or mung; turmeric; ghee and *tadka* spices; basmati; a pan with a tight lid; *atta* flour; a rolling pin; a heavy dry pan; a timer.
**Explanation:**

*Tadka* dal. Simmer split pulses with turmeric until soft and creamy. Season, and finish with a *tadka* poured over at the table. Dried kidney beans (*rajma*) follow the bean rule of §9: soaked for at least 5 hours with the water poured away, then boiled in fresh water for at least 30 minutes, and never cooked in a slow cooker.

*Why ghee and the* tadka *come last.* The spices' aromas are volatile and fat-soluble. Frying them in fat at the end and pouring them over gives the strongest, freshest aroma. Long cooking would drive it off.
*Basmati by absorption:*

items.text: Wash until the water runs almost clear.
Soak for 20–30 minutes; drain.
Cook with a measured amount of water (by the packet, often about 1.5 times the rice's volume) and a tight lid.
Rest off the heat, lid on, before forking.

blocks.text: Don't lift the lid while it cooks: the steam does the work. Leftover rice is cooled fast and kept cold (`SCI-2.M6`).
*Flatbreads:*

items.text: ***chapati*:** wholemeal *atta* flour and water, kneaded and rested, rolled thin, and cooked on a dry hot pan until it puffs (over a flame with tongs, or pressed in the pan with a cloth);
***paratha*:** the same dough layered with ghee and folded, rolled again, and cooked with ghee.

blocks.text: **Practice:**

items.text: ***Dal* and rice (75 min).** A *tadka dal* and basmati by absorption.
**Flatbreads (75 min).** *Chapati* and *paratha*; the *chapati* puffed over a flame or pressed in the pan.

blocks.text: **Look for:** creamy *dal*; long, separate grains; puffed, soft breads.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Wash until the water runs almost clear
The lid lifted; too much heat
Lid on; low heat; rest off the heat
Roll thin; a hot pan; turn quickly
Simmer longer; whisk at the end

blocks.text: **Safety:** the bean rule of §9 for *rajma*; leftover rice cooled fast and in the fridge within 2 hours (`SCI-2.M6`); puffing a *chapati* over a flame with tongs, sleeves clear.
**Record:** the pulses, the rice ratio and soak time, and the photos of the grains and breads.
**Why it matters:** a *thali* gives each dish a small place on one plate, and the eater mixes them in each bite. The skill is contrast: every dish different from its neighbours.
**You need:** the menu; the component table (`FLV-3`); the dishes' ingredients; a large plate or tray with small bowls; the timeline; the household cards.
**Explanation:**
*The* thali. A plate or tray with small portions of several dishes around rice and bread:

items.text: a dry vegetable dish (*sabzi*), for example cabbage or cauliflower with spices, from Dutch seasonal produce;
a *dal*;
a curry;
a *raita*: yoghurt with cucumber or herbs;
a pickle or chutney;
sometimes a sweet.

blocks.text: *Contrast across the plate.* Fill in the component table for the plate:

items.text: **texture:** dry and saucy, soft and crisp;
**heat:** one hot dish, and a cooling *raita*;
**richness:** a rich curry beside a light *dal*;
**colour:** golden *dal*, green herbs, a red curry, white *raita*.

blocks.text: *Planning:*

items.text: the *dal* and the curry ahead: they improve overnight, and are reheated until steaming hot throughout;
the *sabzi* and the breads at the end;
the *raita* in the fridge until serving, then out for at most 2 hours (§9).

blocks.text: *An example, in winter:* a pointed-cabbage *sabzi* with mustard seed and turmeric; a red-lentil *dal*; a chicken curry in a tomato *masala*; basmati and *chapati*; a cucumber-mint *raita*; a lime pickle. The curry is the hot dish, the *raita* cools it, the *sabzi* is dry against the saucy *dal*, and the *chapati* is the soft element.
*Serving.* Fill the small bowls just before serving, rice in the centre and the bread on the side, so nothing sits.
**Practice:**

blocks.text: **Look for:** every dish distinct; a balanced plate.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: One dry *sabzi*; one bread or crisp element
One hot dish; the rest mild

blocks.text: **Safety:** the *raita* out for at most 2 hours (§9); dishes made ahead reheated until steaming hot throughout and not reheated a second time; dairy named for guests.
**Record:** the component table, the photo of the plate, and the cards.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** "Chinese" is not one cuisine. Five regions are enough to start placing a dish by its seasoning and its method, and a balanced meal is judged on texture as much as on taste.

**You need:** light and dark soy sauce, black (Chinkiang) vinegar, Shaoxing wine, Sichuan pepper, chilli bean paste (*doubanjiang*), sesame oil; cucumbers or a seasonal green; garlic; the lens template; tasting forms.
**Explanation:**
*Regional cuisines.* Traditionally there are eight great cuisines; five are a start:

items.text: **Cantonese** (Guangdong): fresh and light; steaming and quick stir-frying, *dim sum*, roast meats;
**Sichuan:** numbing Sichuan pepper with chilli (*mala*), fermented bean paste, bold layered flavour;
**Hunan:** fresh and dried chilli, smoked and cured meats, sour pickles;
**Shanghai** (Jiangnan): sweet-savoury red-braising with soy and sugar, Shaoxing wine, delicate river fish;
**Beijing** and the north: wheat (noodles, dumplings, buns), lamb, roast duck.

blocks.text: *Balance and texture.* A meal balances tastes (salty, sweet, sour, bitter, umami, and in Sichuan the numbing *ma*), methods, and textures: crisp, tender, slippery, chewy. Texture is often valued as much as flavour.

*Wok hei.* The "breath of the wok": a smoky, seared flavour from very high heat, small batches and constant movement. On a home stove it is only partly possible: heat the wok until it smokes, and cook small amounts.
*The pantry:*

items.text: **sauces:** light soy (for seasoning) and dark soy (mostly for colour); oyster sauce; chilli bean paste;
**vinegar and wine:** rice vinegar, black Chinkiang vinegar, Shaoxing wine;
**aromatics:** ginger, garlic, spring onion;
**dried goods:** dried mushrooms, fermented black beans, Sichuan pepper, star anise;
**sesame oil,** a finishing oil, not a cooking oil; **cornflour** for velveting and sauces.

blocks.text: *Meal structure and drinks.* Rice (or noodles, or buns) with several shared dishes, and a soup; tea. Chinese-Indonesian restaurant food in the Netherlands is its own tradition, related but distinct.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A flavour tasting (60 min).** Light and dark soy, black vinegar, Shaoxing wine, Sichuan pepper and chilli bean paste tasted. Then one simple dish (a smashed cucumber salad in summer, or quick-braised greens) seasoned two regional ways: for example Sichuan (chilli oil, Sichuan pepper, black vinegar) and Cantonese (light soy, ginger, a little sesame oil).

blocks.text: **Look for:** you can place a dish by its seasoning and method.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Dark soy used as a seasoning
Light soy to season; dark soy for colour
Sesame oil at the end, a few drops
Choose a region; season by its profile

blocks.text: **Safety:** soy, sesame, wheat (check the soy sauce's label), fish and crustaceans (oyster sauce, dried shrimp) named for guests.
**Record:** the tasting form, the two seasonings of the same dish, and the regional placing.
**Why it matters:** a stir-fry takes minutes, so it is won or lost in the preparation. On a home stove, the batches and the heat decide whether the food sears or steams.

**You need:** a flat-bottomed carbon-steel wok or a large heavy pan; the biggest burner (on induction, a flat wok); the protein (chicken, pork or beef); soy, Shaoxing wine, cornflour, egg white or oil; seasonal vegetables (pointed cabbage, leeks, green beans, mushrooms); a lid; small bowls; the probe.
**Explanation:**
*Prep everything first* (`WRK-1`):

items.text: every ingredient cut to a similar size;
the sauce mixed in a bowl;
everything lined up, in the order it goes in.

blocks.text: *Velveting.* Thin slices of chicken, pork or beef marinated briefly in soy, Shaoxing wine, cornflour and a little egg white or oil, then flashed in oil or water. The meat comes out tender and silky.
*Wok heat on a home stove:*

items.text: Heat the wok until it smokes before the oil goes in.
Cook in small batches, so the wok stays hot: a crowded wok steams.
Sear the protein and lift it out; cook the vegetables; put everything back together.

blocks.text: *The sauce at the end.* Pour the premixed sauce (soy, wine, stock, sugar, cornflour) in at the end, and toss until it is glossy and coats. Stir the bowl just before pouring: cornflour settles, and a settled sauce goes in as lumps.
*Doneness.* Chicken is cooked to 75 °C; pork and beef slices are cooked through for a family meal. Probe a thick piece from each batch.
**Practice:**

items.text: **A stir-fry (75 min).** A velveted chicken or pork stir-fry with seasonal vegetables, the batches timed.

blocks.text: **Look for:** seared, not steamed; vegetables bright and crisp-tender; a glossy sauce that coats.

**Why it matters:** dumplings and steamed fish are the moist methods of the Chinese kitchen. The dough's water temperature decides how it rolls and cooks; the probe decides when the filling and the fish are done.

**You need:** plain flour, boiling water; minced pork or chicken, or mushrooms, cabbage and tofu; ginger, spring onion, soy, Shaoxing wine, sesame oil; a whole fish (a North Sea fish or a Dutch-farmed trout); a steamer; a pan with a lid; the probe.
**Explanation:**
*Hot-water against cold-water dough:*

items.text: **hot water** partly cooks the starch and weakens the gluten: a soft, tender dough, easy to roll thin, for steamed and pan-fried dumplings;
**cold water** keeps the gluten strong: a chewier dough that holds up to boiling.

blocks.text: *The filling.* Minced pork (or chicken, or a vegetarian mix of mushrooms, cabbage and tofu) with ginger, spring onion, soy, Shaoxing wine and sesame oil, beaten in one direction until sticky. Salt the cabbage and squeeze out its water first; a watery filling bursts the wrapper.
*Two folds:*

items.text: **a half-moon with pleats** along one side;
**a simple pinched fold.**

blocks.text: Seal well, without trapped air.
*Cooking:*

items.text: **boiled:** into boiling water, brought back to the boil with a splash of cold water, until they float and the filling is cooked;
**pan-fried** (*guotie*): browned, then steamed with water under a lid, then crisped again.

blocks.text: A minced-pork filling reaches 75 °C (§9). Cut one dumpling from each batch and probe it.

*Steamed fish with ginger and spring onion.* Steam a whole fish over boiling water until it reaches 63 °C at the bone (§9). Top with shredded ginger and spring onion, pour over smoking oil, and add a light soy dressing.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Dumplings (90 min).** A hot-water dough, a filling, two folds; boiled and pan-fried.
**Steamed fish (60 min).** A whole fish steamed, probed and dressed.

blocks.text: **Look for:** thin, sealed wrappers; a juicy filling at 75 °C; fish just opaque at the bone.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Salt and squeeze the cabbage; beat the filling sticky
Wrapper rolled evenly to the edge
Roll the edges thinner than the centre
Probe early at the thickest point by the bone
Too little oil, lid lifted early
Oil the pan; steam until the water is gone

blocks.text: **Safety:** the filling probed to 75 °C and the fish to 63 °C at the bone (§9); steam lid lifted away from you; hot oil poured slowly over the fish.
**Record:** the dough, the probe readings for each batch, and photos of the folds and the fish.
**Why it matters:** in a Chinese family meal the balance is in the table, not on the plate. Three dishes made by different methods, around rice, also need to reach the table hot together.
**You need:** rice; the ingredients for three dishes of different methods; the steamer, the wok and a braising pot; the timeline; the probe; the household cards.
**Explanation:**
*The table.* Rice for everyone, and three or more dishes shared, for example:

items.text: a stir-fry;
a steamed or braised dish;
a vegetable dish;
perhaps a soup.

blocks.text: *Balance of the table, not the plate:*

items.text: **methods:** stir-fried, steamed, braised;
**main ingredients:** meat, fish, vegetable, tofu;
**textures and tastes:** one spicy, one mild, one sour.

blocks.text: The rice is the centre: each dish is seasoned to be eaten with plain rice, so it can be saltier than a dish eaten on its own.
*Timing.* The braised dish is made ahead: it holds, and many braises improve. The steamed dish goes in the steamer while the wok heats. The stir-fry is last and fast, and goes straight to the table.
*An example, in autumn:*

items.text: a red-braised pork belly (Shanghai), made the day before;
a steamed trout with ginger and spring onion;
stir-fried pointed cabbage with garlic and black vinegar;

blocks.text: Three methods, three main ingredients, and three tastes: rich and sweet-savoury, delicate, and sharp. The pork is reheated while the fish steams; the cabbage takes a few minutes at the end.
*Serving.* Everything goes on the table at once, with a bowl of rice for each person; the dishes are shared, each eater taking a little at a time.

Seasoned as a dish on its own

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** *dashi* is the stock under most Japanese cooking, and it is made in minutes, not hours. It carries umami and aroma rather than body, which is why the Western stock habits of `STK-2` spoil it.
**You need:** *kombu*, *katsuobushi* (dried bonito flakes), dried shiitake; cold water; a pan; a fine sieve lined with cloth or kitchen paper; a thermometer; salt and soy for tasting; tasting forms.
**Explanation:**
*Seasonality (*shun*) and restraint.* Ingredients at their peak, cooked to show their own flavour. Small portions, many textures, and attention to presentation and the season.
*Umami as the backbone.* *Kombu* brings glutamate and *katsuobushi* brings inosinate; together they give the synergy of `TST-1.M3.L4` and `FLV-3.M3`: more umami than either alone.
*The first* dashi:

items.text: Soak the *kombu* in cold water.
Heat it gently, and take it out just before the boil. Boiled *kombu* turns slimy and bitter.
Add the *katsuobushi* off the heat, steep for a few minutes, and strain without pressing. Squeezed flakes make it cloudy and fishy.

blocks.text: It should be clear, pale gold and delicate.
*The other* dashi:

items.text: **a second *dashi*** (*niban dashi*): the used *kombu* and flakes simmered again in fresh water for a stronger, coarser stock, used for simmering;
**a vegetarian *dashi*:** *kombu* with dried shiitake, soaked in cold water.

blocks.text: *How it differs from Western stock* (`STK-2`): minutes rather than hours; no bones and no browning; no gelatin. It is an infusion that carries umami and aroma, not body. Simmered for an hour, it goes bitter and murky.
*The pantry:* soy sauce, *mirin*, sake, rice vinegar, white and red miso, *kombu*, *katsuobushi*, dried shiitake, short-grain rice, sesame, *nori*, pickles.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Three *dashi* (60 min).** A *kombu*-*katsuobushi dashi*, a second *dashi* from its leftovers, and a *kombu*-shiitake *dashi*. Taste each plain, then with a pinch of salt and a few drops of soy.

blocks.text: **Look for:** a clear, delicate *dashi*; the umami obvious once salted.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Let them drain on their own
Taste with a pinch of salt; the umami appears

blocks.text: **Safety:** fish (bonito), soy and sesame named for guests; the *dashi* cooled and in the fridge within 2 hours if kept (§9).
**Record:** the three *dashi*, the tasting notes plain and salted, and the photos of their colour.
**Why it matters:** *ichijū sansai*, "one soup, three dishes", is the shape of a Japanese home meal. It teaches the rice, the miso soup, and the habit of small, distinct dishes.

**You need:** Japanese short-grain rice; a pan with a tight lid; *dashi*; white or red miso; tofu, wakame and spring onion, or seasonal Dutch vegetables (leek, spinach, turnip, mushrooms); greens for *ohitashi*; sesame seeds; a cucumber or cabbage for a quick pickle; small bowls and a tray.
**Explanation:**
*The set meal.* Rice, miso soup and three small dishes, each in its own bowl or plate on a tray:

items.text: **a main:** often grilled fish or a simmered dish;
**two sides:** for example a dressed vegetable and a pickle.

blocks.text: *The rice:*

items.text: Wash the short-grain rice until the water runs almost clear, to remove surface starch.
Soak for about 30 minutes.
Cook with a measured amount of water (by the packet) and a tight lid.
Rest for 10 minutes off the heat.

blocks.text: It should be sticky but with distinct grains. Leftover rice is cooled fast and kept cold (`SCI-2.M6`).

*Miso soup.* Heat the *dashi* with the tofu, wakame or vegetables until they are cooked. Then take it off the boil and dissolve the miso in a ladle of the broth before stirring it in. Boiling dulls the miso's aroma. Finish with spring onion.
*Small dishes:*

items.text: ***ohitashi*:** blanched greens squeezed and dressed with *dashi* and soy;
***goma-ae*:** blanched greens with a sesame dressing;
**a quick pickle:** cucumber or cabbage salted and pressed.

blocks.text: *Portions.* Each dish is small: a few mouthfuls. The tray is varied rather than large.
**Practice:**

items.text: **Rice and miso soup (60 min).** Rice by absorption; miso soup with seasonal vegetables.
**The side dishes (75 min).** Two small vegetable dishes and a quick pickle; the tray set.

blocks.text: **Look for:** glossy, sticky rice with distinct grains; miso soup not boiled; each dish small and distinct.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Wash until the water runs almost clear
Off the boil; dissolve it in a ladle
Each dish served as a main

blocks.text: **Safety:** leftover rice cooled fast and in the fridge within 2 hours (`SCI-2.M6`); soy, sesame and fish named for guests.
**Record:** the rice ratio and soak, the photo of the tray, and the tasting notes.

blocks.text: **Why it matters:** *nimono* and *yakimono* are the simmered and grilled dishes of the set meal. Both depend on order: the order the seasonings go in, and when the glaze goes on.

**You need:** seasonal Dutch roots (turnip, carrot, pumpkin, potato) and mushrooms; *dashi*; sugar, salt, soy, *mirin*; a drop lid (*otoshibuta*) or a circle of baking paper; a whole mackerel or fillets, or chicken thighs; the grill or a heavy pan; the probe.
**Explanation:**

*Nimono.* Vegetables simmered gently in seasoned *dashi* under a drop lid: a lid that rests on the food, keeping it submerged and the pieces from tumbling. They absorb the seasoning and stay intact. Dutch roots fit well: turnip for daikon, carrot, pumpkin, potato, mushrooms.
*The* sa-shi-su-se-so *order:*

items.text: sugar (*sa*);
salt (*shi*);
vinegar (*su*);
soy sauce (*se*, an old spelling);
miso (*so*).

blocks.text: Sugar goes first because its larger molecules penetrate slowly, and salt firms the food. Soy and miso go last because their aroma fades with heat.
*Yakimono:*

items.text: ***shioyaki*,** salt-grilled fish: a whole mackerel or fillets salted 20–30 minutes ahead, then grilled until the skin is crisp and the fish is cooked to 63 °C at the bone;
***teriyaki*:** chicken thighs or fish glazed with soy, *mirin* and sugar. The glaze goes on near the end, so it doesn't burn. Chicken is cooked to 75 °C.

blocks.text: *Seasoning by taste* (`FL-SEAS`). Taste each dish before serving, adjust the balance, and note the adjustment: a *nimono* that needs a little more soy, a *teriyaki* glaze that is too sweet.
**Practice:**

items.text: ***Nimono* (60 min).** Seasonal roots simmered under a drop lid, seasoned in order.
***Yakimono* (60 min).** Salt-grilled mackerel or a chicken *teriyaki*, probed.

blocks.text: **Look for:** vegetables intact and seasoned through; crisp-skinned fish at 63 °C; a glossy glaze, not burnt.
**If it goes wrong:**

rows: Soy at the start of a long simmer
Sugar first; soy near the end
A drop lid; a gentle simmer
Cook first; glaze at the end

blocks.text: **Safety:** fish to 63 °C at the bone and chicken to 75 °C (§9); the grill tray's fat watched, and a lid at hand.
**Record:** the seasoning order with amounts, the adjustments, and the probe readings.
**Why it matters:** the Japanese home kitchen wastes little: leftover rice and fish become lunch. That only works inside the time limits of §9, and with an egg cooked for the eater.

**You need:** freshly cooked or properly stored short-grain rice; chicken, beef and onion, or tofu; *dashi*, soy, *mirin*; eggs; fillings for *onigiri* (salted salmon, a pickled plum, a cooked vegetable); *nori*; salt; cucumber, cabbage, radish or turnip for pickles; the probe.
**Explanation:**
*Donburi.* A bowl of rice with a simmered or grilled topping:

items.text: ***oyakodon*:** chicken and egg simmered in seasoned *dashi*;
***gyūdon*:** beef and onion;
**a vegetable or tofu version.**

blocks.text: The topping moistens the rice without drowning it. Chicken is cooked to 75 °C. **A soft-set egg is not served to risk groups (§9);** for them it is cooked through.

*Onigiri.* Rice balls shaped with wet, salted hands around a filling, and wrapped in *nori*. The rice must be warm and sticky enough to shape. *Onigiri* are eaten the same day and kept cool; cooked rice follows the rules of §9.
*Tsukemono.* Quick pickles of cucumber, cabbage, radish or turnip with salt (and *kombu*, rice vinegar or miso), ready in hours, kept in the fridge.
*Using leftovers the Japanese way:*

items.text: leftover rice as *onigiri*, fried rice or rice porridge;
leftover grilled fish flaked into *onigiri*;
a little leftover simmered dish on a *donburi*;
always within the 2-day limit (§9). Write the day each leftover was cooked on its box.

Too much liquid in the topping
Reduce the topping; spoon it on

A soft egg for a pregnant guest
